figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: In-context learning protocol. For each task, GPT-6-Astra studies the training data and writes a knowledge package $K$, which is frozen before testing. Each test episode starts a fresh session with $K$ and runs under the standard ($1\times$) or extended ($10\times$) budget. Model weights remain fixed throughout, and $K$ remains unchanged during testing, and no information passes between episodes.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Success rate versus step budget. The budget is expressed as a multiple of each benchmark’s official step limit; dots show observed success rates and pink curves show fitted trends. We evaluate budgets up to $10\times$ the official limit ($1\times$ for BEHAVIOR). The gray line marks the upper bound, which assumes that every episode that exhausts the evaluated budget without succeeding has the potential to succeed with an unlimited budget.
figures.headline: Success rises as the step budget grows, and observed rates stay below an upper bound.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: (a) Average per-task token usage and (b) average per-task time for each benchmark, stacked from bottom to top as ICL preparation, the $1\times$ run, and the additional cost of extending to $10\times$. Here, $1\times$ and $10\times$ denote maximum action-step budgets, not token or time budgets. The relatively small additional token and time costs primarily reflect early termination of extended runs upon success or terminal failure, before the full $10\times$ budget is exhausted. We observe that the vast majority of tokens consumed are cached input tokens (approximately 98% in our runs). Accordingly, we use a simple rule of thumb for cost estimation: 1M tokens $\approx$ 1 USD.
figures.headline: Extending the budget from 1× to 10× adds comparatively small token and time costs, mainly from early termination.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Residual failures under ICL with the extended budget. Each pair shows the state before a key event and its outcome; purple arrows mark the relevant objects. (a) Verifying physical success: apparent or self-reported completion diverges from the actual task state. (b) Recovering from consequential actions: an early mishap, such as a spill or a dropped part, cannot be undone and derails later subtasks. (c) Preserving progress over long horizons: progress that later steps depend on, such as an open lid or a placed object, is lost and blocks the task.
figures.headline: Residual failures fall into three types: unverified completion, irreversible mishaps, and lost progress over long horizons.

abstract:
GPT-6-Astra demonstrates a level of competence in robotic manipulation and navigation that challenges the conventional paradigm of building specialized models for individual tasks and embodiments. In this report, we ask not only how capable GPT-6-Astra is, but what its capabilities imply for the field. First, we probe the limits of standalone GPT-6-Astra. We conduct a large-scale evaluation across 12 representative benchmarks spanning tabletop manipulation, humanoids, mobile platforms, and dexterous hands. Under a unified protocol that allows in-context learning (ICL) from training-set demonstrations and substantially increases the number of execution steps, GPT-6-Astra achieves unprecedented performance (Fig. 1). Our analysis suggests that future research should increasingly focus on improving 1) the generality of in-context learning 2) cost and execution time, 3) physical-state verification, 4) recovery from irreversible failures, and 5) long-horizon preservation of progress. Second, we study the agentic harness for embodied control. Besides exploring the ideal action representation and chucking parameters, we identify that close-loop coordination between a high-level "System 2" reasoner (i.e., GPT-6-Astra) and a low-level "System 1" controller (e.g., $\pi_{0.5}$) is costly but effective. Third, we examine GPT-6-Astra on real-world deployment. Our experiments on 8 robot configurations reveal substantial gaps: 1) robot demonstrations required for in-context learning are expensive to collect, and 2) it is implausible to trade longer execution for higher success rates with physical constraints. Fourth, we envision the next generation of embodied benchmarks. We develop a prototype that 1) derives tasks from real-world needs rather than current robot capabilities, 2) provides no in-domain demonstrations, and 3) judges agents on a world clock that keeps running while they deliberate. Taken together, our results suggest that GPT-6-Astra has largely crossed the threshold of embodied competence, but not yet that of practical embodied intelligence. The key remaining challenge is to translate benchmark success into reliable, efficient, and scalable real-world deployment.

sections.body: The report starts from a unified protocol that allows in-context learning from training demonstrations and extends the step budget up to 10× the official setting. Across 12 benchmarks covering tabletop arms, humanoids, mobile platforms and dexterous hands, the model reaches 81.9% on RoboDojo and 87.3% on DexJoCo, and approaches saturation on the LIBERO series and SIMPLE. The authors then ablate the harness that pairs the model with a low-level controller, and validate findings on real robots. They also propose principles for next-generation embodied benchmarks. The stated limits include weak transfer of in-context knowledge beyond the demonstrated tasks, high inference cost, unreliable physical verification, poor recovery from irreversible failures, and loss of progress over long horizons.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: The report asks what a general model's embodied competence implies, and where the field should go next.

sections.body: The model's weights stay fixed. For each task, it studies the training demonstrations and writes a knowledge package that is frozen before testing, and each test episode starts fresh with that package. Two budgets are compared: the standard budget prescribed by each benchmark, and an extended budget of up to 10× the standard number of action steps. On SIMPLE, task-level in-context learning raises standard-budget success on four common tasks from 70.8% to 90.8%. The benefit depends on how closely the training data covers the test tasks. Success approaches saturation where tasks follow the training distribution, and stays moderate on RoboLab, which has no training set. Extending the budget yields large gains on RoboDojo and Bench2Dex. Residual failures include unverified completion, irreversible mishaps, and lost progress over long horizons.
sections.heading: Large-Scale Study under A Unified Protocol
sections.headline: At the standard budget, the model matches or exceeds the best published result on most of twelve settings.

sections.body: The harness ablation pairs the model with a low-level controller, $\pi_{0.5}$ as the controller on RoboDojo. The standalone controller averages 6.91% success, and open-loop collaboration averages 5.83% using 0.387 million tokens. In closed-loop review, the model accepts, modifies or rejects each proposed action. Per-action review costs 7.664 million tokens. Reviewing four actions per call cuts tokens by 63.5% to 2.796 million and raises success from 23.61% to 25.83%. Adding in-context learning to closed-loop review reaches 54.17% at 19.335 million tokens. For action interfaces, directional commands add 2.50 percentage points, while direct joint-angle control drops 5.84 points. Adaptive chunking adds 4.44 points at 1.146 million tokens, while fixed chunks of four lose 4.17 points.
sections.heading: Harness Ablation
sections.headline: Closed-loop review improves success by up to 20.00 percentage points over open-loop execution, at higher token cost.

sections.body: The real-world variant removes demonstrations and step budgets. The model works zero-shot from human-written context, and each trial normally gets 60 minutes of wall-clock time, with a person judging success from the physical outcome. Eight platforms across five embodiment classes were tested. Rigid pick-and-place succeeded in 17/18 trials, while cloth folding reached 2/4 on the Franka 3. Flower insertion succeeded on the dual-arm Piper only after the free arm moved to bring the vase mouth into view. On the Unitree G1, the model commands existing motor controllers: manipulation succeeded in 2/3 trials and locomotion in 3/3. The stated limits are safety stops, mechanical overheating, and time. About 90% of a G1 run is deliberation, and without grasp primitives the Tianji hands completed 0/3 grasps.
sections.heading: Real-World Validation
sections.headline: Zero-shot control succeeded in 17/18 rigid pick-and-place trials but 0/11 plug insertion trials.

sections.body: Current benchmarks assume demonstrations of the test task, a fully specified goal, and a world that waits for the agent. The section proposes three principles: derive tasks from human needs and judge utility rather than fixed goal states; provide no in-domain demonstrations, so agents learn at test time; and keep the world running while the agent deliberates. A household prototype in a simulated apartment tested the model on need-based tasks with no demonstrations. Five representative runs failed. The robot lost track of changes it caused, such as a refrigerator door left open from 300 s to 765 s of world time. It did not work out how to position its body for an open door. It also acted on observations that had become outdated, and an egg charred about 90 s after it set. The authors note these episodes are few and qualitative.
sections.heading: Towards a Next-Generation Embodied Benchmark
sections.headline: Current benchmarks were designed for imitation-trained policies, so the report proposes three principles for next-generation designs.

sections.body: The conclusion is that GPT-6-Astra represents a clear advance in embodied intelligence, but not its endpoint. Strong harness design, in-context learning and a sufficient execution budget push many isolated benchmarks close to saturation. The remaining challenges shift toward transfer across tasks, long-horizon reasoning, failure recovery, and real-world constraints on time, cost and safety. The authors argue that benchmark success should be interpreted with more care, and that the next goal is embodied systems that operate reliably and efficiently under realistic deployment conditions.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: GPT-6-Astra is a clear advance in embodied capability, but benchmark success does not yet imply reliable deployment.

sections.body: The appendix begins with the project contributors and advisory board. It then gives related work on foundation models as embodied agents, robot policy learning, and embodied benchmarks, followed by a survey of empirical studies of frontier models in embodied settings. Per-platform real-world results follow, with setup, context provided, tasks and results, and findings for each platform, including the Franka, PiPER, Tianji, Galaxea, AgileX Tracer and Unitree G1 systems. The last figures, 13 to 21, show a gallery of zero-shot real-world tasks grouped by outcome, along with per-platform visualizations.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists contributors, related work, empirical studies of frontier models, and per-platform real-world results.
